title: Quantum mechanics in configuration space in context
authors: Arwa Bukhari, Margherita Moro, Max Davies, Alastair Wilson, Almut Beige
abstract: To enhance the way in which wave-particle duality is implemented in the modelling of quantum mechanical systems, Bukhari et al. [New J. Phys. 27, 084501 (2025)] recently introduced an alternative approach to quantum mechanics, namely quantum mechanics in configuration space. This formalism is based on a physically motivated quantisation of Newtonian mechanics and promotes the classical position-velocity states (x,v) to pairwise distinguishable quantum states. The resulting |x,v> states form the basis of the Hilbert space of individual quantum mechanical particles and evolve along classical trajectories. In this paper, we consider the modelling of a mechanical particle in free space and put quantum mechanics in configuration space into context. It is shown that this formalism increases the continuity between quantum and classical mechanics by avoiding a conceptual inconsistency associated with the definition of momentum in canonical quantisation. In addition, we emphasise that standard quantum mechanics and quantum mechanics in configuration space are based on two distinct formulations of classical mechanics.
summary: The paper proposes Quantum Mechanics in Configuration Space (QMCS) as an alternative formalism to improve the conceptual link between QM and CM. By quantizing based on Newtonian mechanics using position-velocity states, QMCS supports independent observables like velocity ($\hat{v}$), which is often lost in standard canonical quantization. This suggests a more physically transparent quantum theory derived from classical principles.
main_problem: The paper addresses enhancing the conceptual continuity between quantum mechanics (QM) and classical mechanics (CM) by proposing an alternative formalism: Quantum Mechanics in Configuration Space (QMCS). It aims to resolve inconsistencies arising from standard canonical quantization.
main_result: QMCS, which quantizes based on Newtonian mechanics using position-velocity states $|x, v\rangle$, provides a framework that maintains strong conceptual continuity with classical dynamics and supports independent observables for velocity ($\hat{v}$) and acceleration ($\hat{a}$).
method: The authors compare three formulations of CM (Newtonian, Lagrangian, Hamiltonian) to determine the most physically transparent quantization procedure. They then derive the quantum dynamics using a basis built on $(x, v)$ states.
model_or_system: The model is a single mechanical particle moving in free space along one dimension ($x$). The formalism compares standard QM (based on canonical commutation relations) against QMCS (based on Newtonian mechanics).
key_observables: Position ($\hat{x}$), velocity ($\hat{v}$), momentum ($\hat{p}$), and acceleration ($\hat{a}$) are key observables, with the paper deriving new commutation relations like $[\hat{v}, \hat{a}] = i\hbar$.
important_parameters: The fundamental constant $\hbar$ governs the quantum corrections; the analysis focuses on the free space limit ($V(x)=0$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that Newtonian mechanics provides the most physically perspicuous starting point for quantization. It also assumes QMCS can be compatible with various measurement interpretations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual relationship between different CM formulations and show how QMCS maintains a stronger link to classical dynamics compared to standard QM approaches.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem by comparing CM frameworks (Newtonian vs. Hamiltonian). It then introduces QMCS using the $(x, v)$ basis states. Finally, it derives the quantum dynamics for free space and contrasts its results with standard QM predictions regarding observable consistency.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to foundational theoretical physics, particularly concerning the precise mathematical structure required to bridge classical intuition (like velocity) into a fully consistent quantum description beyond standard canonical quantization rules.

Illustration of four different sets of basis states which are all linked via Fourier transforms and which can be used interchangeably to describe a single quantum mechanical par- ticle moving along the x-axis. The most classical among the quantum basis states are the |x, v⟩states which correspond directly to the (x, v) states of Newtonian mechanics. In con- trast to this, the |p, a⟩states, are the least classical quantum bases, since they are equal superpositions of all |x, v⟩states. Such states do not exist in CM.

The classical-quantum ‘conceptual continuity’ flows upward in the chart, i.e. the ‘conceptual continuity’ between QMCS and Newtonian mechanics is more enhanced than the conceptual continuity between SQM and Hamiltonian mechanics.
